name: Scottish English (Scottish Standard English and Scots)
summary: Scottish English covers a range of speech from Scottish Standard English (SSE), the formal variety used in Scotland, to Scots, a separate Germanic language closely related to English that sits at the broad end of a continuum. Most middle-class speakers conform to standard grammar and use SSE in formal settings and Scots-influenced speech informally. The most useful features for an actor are sound features: rhoticity (r is pronounced), the /hw/ versus /w/ distinction in 'which' and 'witch', the Scottish Vowel Length Rule (vowels before voiced sounds are longer), the pull-pool merger, and the 'ch' sound in 'loch'. Grammar and vocabulary differences are fewer and mostly come from Scots. Sources are Wikipedia articles on Scottish English, the Scottish Vowel Length Rule and Scots. Scots-specific words such as 'och', 'ken' and 'dinnae' were NOT found in the opened sources and are deliberately left out.

pronunciation.rule: Rhoticity: Scottish English is mostly rhotic, so /r/ is pronounced in the syllable coda (after a vowel, at the end of a word or before a consonant).
pronunciation.ipa: /r/ in coda pronounced (realisation varies by speaker)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Pronounce every r you see after a vowel: 'car', 'hard', 'bird', 'worst'. Do not drop it. Keep it clear rather than soft.

pronunciation.rule: W and wh are distinct in many speakers: 'which' starts with a /hw/ sound while 'witch' starts with a plain /w/.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Breathe a little puff of air before the w in 'which', 'whale', 'whisky' so it starts like 'hw'. 'Witch' and 'wind' start with a plain w, no puff.
pronunciation.example: which vs witch; whale vs wail

pronunciation.rule: Scottish Vowel Length Rule: a vowel is phonetically longer before voiced fricatives (v, z, th as in 'this', zh), before /r/, and before a morpheme boundary; it is shorter before the voiceless counterparts.
pronunciation.ipa: [seːv] save vs [sef] safe; [doːz] doze vs [dos] dose; [tiːð] teethe vs [tiθ] teeth
pronunciation.actor_tip: Lengthen the vowel before voiced sounds (v, z, 'th' in 'this'). 'Save' has a longer vowel than 'safe'; 'doze' is longer than 'dose'. Keep the length moderate; this is about length, not stress or emphasis. Note that 'need' stays short but 'kneed' (the past of 'knee' used as a verb) is longer, showing the rule responds to word structure.
pronunciation.example: save / safe; doze / dose; teethe / teeth; need / kneed

pronunciation.rule: Pull-pool merger: Scottish English has no /ʊ/ and uses Scots /u/ instead, so 'pull' and 'pool' are homophones (sound the same).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Say 'pull' with the same vowel as 'pool' (the long 'oo'). Do not use the short 'uh'-like vowel of standard English.

pronunciation.rule: BATH, TRAP and PALM share the same open 'a' vowel in many Scottish speakers, so they do not get the long RP-style 'bahth' vowel.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Use the same short open 'a' as in 'cat' for 'bath', 'path' and 'palm'. Do not lengthen 'bath' into 'bahth'.

pronunciation.rule: Loch sound: the ch in 'loch' (and some Scots words) is a voiceless velar fricative, made at the back of the throat.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Make a soft 'kh' sound with the back of the tongue near the soft palate, like a gentle throat clear. Use only in words that have this sound in the text (loch, Gaelic-derived names). Do not add it to ordinary 'ch' words like 'church'.

common_mistakes: Putting 'och', 'aye', 'ken', 'dinnae' and similar Scots words into every line. Only 'aye' is verified here; the others need checking before use.
Applying the Scottish Vowel Length Rule as a stressed drawl. It is a length difference, not emphasis.
Rolling the r heavily in every word. Rhotic means the r is pronounced, not that it is trilled throughout.
Using a 'Highland' or 'Braveheart' accent for a Glasgow or Edinburgh character. Scottish accents differ strongly by region.
Using Scots vocabulary for a formal or professional character. SSE is the formal variety.
Applying the loch sound to every 'ch'.
generational_notes: The source describes Scots as informal and Scottish Standard English as the formal variety, with many speakers switching between them.
Source does not give clear age-based decline figures for Scots or SSE; treat generational claims as unverified until checked.
The Scottish Vowel Length Rule article notes that some Scots dialects, including Northern Scots and Shetland, apply the rule less consistently; regional spread of other features was not verified.
conversion_guidelines: Decide the register first: formal or professional character uses SSE (no Scots vocabulary, standard grammar, sound features only). Informal, working-class or rural characters can take Scots vocabulary.
Apply sound features first: rhoticity, /hw/ in wh-words, pull-pool, and the Scottish Vowel Length Rule. These are the safest and most accurate.
Use at most one or two grammar items per monologue (needs washed; wait on).
Use aye and wee where they fit naturally. Use bairn/wean only for children, chosen by region.
Apply the loch sound only to words spelled with ch that the text uses as loch-type words.
Do not add 'och', 'ken' or 'dinnae' unless the user supplies a verified source for them.
In stage notes, mark the register (SSE or Scots) and the region if known, because Scottish speech differs greatly by place.
